docs.title: Glossary
docs.text:
Integer A numeric value without a decimal, e.g., 10

Float A numeric value with a decimal, e.g., 10.0

String A sequence of characters enclosed in quotes

Boolean A data type representing true or false

None A special data type in Python denoting no value, NoneType

Variable A label that points to a memory location storing data

print() A function to output text to the console in Python

Concatination Joining strings together using the + operator

Comment Non-executable text in the code, marked by #

input() A function to take user input as a string in Python

Case Sensitive Python's distinction between uppercase and lowercase letters

Typecasting Converting a variable from one data type to another

Boolean Casting For empty strings or 0, returns False; else True

Integer to Boolean 0 converts to False, others to True

String to Boolean Empty string converts to False, non-empty to True

Float to Integer Rounds towards zero, e.g., 3.99 becomes 3

Arithmetic Operators Include +, -, *, /, %, //, and **

Comparison Operators ==, !=, <, >, <=, >= used for comparisons

Logical Operators Combine conditions, include and, or, not

Assignment Operator Assigns values, denoted by =

Control Statements Decide execution flow, like if, else, elif

Nested if An if inside another if, creating multiple layers

docs.title: Installation
docs.text: Status: In Progress

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Python is a programming language and our computer needs a program called Interpreter to read and run Python code.

Installing Python means, installing the interpreter plus the pip, the tool that downloads extra libraries.

docs.title: Step1: Check if Python is already installed
docs.text:
• Open command prompt and type python --version and press Enter.
  • If you see something like Python 3.3.x, its installed.
  • If it errors out then probably it's not installed.

docs.title: Step2: Download the installer
docs.text:
• Go to www.python.org/downloads
  • Download the latest version.

docs.title: Step3: Run the Installer
docs.text: • On the first screen, tick the box "Add python.exe to PATH". This is the most important step. PATH is a list of folders that Windows will search when we type a command.

docs.title: Step4: Verify it worked
docs.text: • Open command prompt and verify python --version and pip --version

docs.title: Step5: Run the first program
docs.text:
• Type python and press enter. You'll see >>> which is the interactive mode.
  • Type print("Hello World!") and press Enter.
  • Type exit() to leave.

docs.title: Installing Python on Linux
docs.text: Most Linux Distributions comes pre-installed with Python as their system tools depend on it.

docs.title: Step1: Check the current version
docs.text: • Open a terminal and run python --version

docs.title: Step2: Installing or upgrading using the package manager
docs.text:
Distribution Command Ubuntu, Debian, Mint sudo apt update then sudo apt install python3 python3-pip python3-venv Fedora sudo dnf install python3 python3-pip Arch, Manjaro sudo pacman -S python python-pip

sudo means run as administrator

docs.title: Step3: Verify
docs.text:
• Run python3 --version and pip3 --version

Don't touch the system Python. Instead, use a version manager uv or virtual environment.

docs.title: Step4: Virtual environments
docs.text:
• A virtual environment is a private folder holding Python libraries for one project, so they never conflict. 
        python -m venv .venv
    source .venv/bin/activate
  • When active we will see (.veve) at the start of prompt. Now any pip install requests installs only into this folder.
  • Type deactivate to leave.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: Status: Completed

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Python is an open-source easy to learn high-level programming language. It was developed by Guido Van Rossum in 1993. The language is engineered to let programmers focus on finding solutions to problems.

Written in plain english, It is easy to code and improves productivity. It has a vast library support.

Python can be used almost anywhere and offers lots of career options.

docs.title: Key features of Python
docs.text:
1. Simple and Easy to Learn: Python has an uncluttered, minimalistic syntax and English like key-words. Fewer lines of code.
  2. High-level Language: Programmers do not have to manage low-level system details, such as manual memory management.
  3. Interpreted and Dynamic: Python does not require source code to be compiled into binary machine code ahead of time. The interpreter converts code into an intermediate format known as bytecode and executes it line-by-line, providing instant feedback in an interactive shell or terminal.
  4. Multi-paradigm: Python supports procedure-oriented programming as well as a flexible implementation of object-oriented programming (OOP). In Python, everything—including numbers, strings, and functions—is treated as an object.
  5. Cross-Platform Portability: Python runs seamlessly across major operating systems, including Linux, Windows, macOS, and Unix variants. Code written without platform-specific dependencies works across different environments without modification.
  6. "Batteries Included" Standard Library: Every standard Python distribution includes an extensive standard library offering built-in modules for mathematics, regular expressions, system calls, threading, file handling, unit testing, and internet protocols.
  7. Expansive Third-Party Ecosystem: Beyond the standard library, thousands of external libraries and packages are available via the Python Package Index (PyPI) and can be installed using the pip package manager.
  8. Free and Open Source Software: Python is maintained as a Free and Open Source Software (FLOSS) project, steered by the Python Software Foundation and supported by a diverse, active global community.

docs.title: Major use cases
docs.text:
1. Automation & Task Scripting: Python is widely used to automate repetitive, administrative and system tasks with Built-in-modules, BeautifulSoup and Scrapy.
  2. Web Development: Python powers robust, interactive websites and scalable web applications through modern web frameworks such as Django and Flask.
  3. Data Analysis and Visualization: Python is primary tool used across scientific research, business intelligence and academic work with specialized libraries like Matplotlib, Pandas, NumPy and Plotly.
  4. Web Scraping and API Consumption: Programs can automate data collection from the internet by downloading pages and parsing HTML with tools such as Requests, Beautiful Soup, and Selenium. It can also be used to interact with REST APIs and process structured formats like JSON and CSV.
  5. Game Development: With multimedia libraries such as PyGame, Python is used to build 2D video games, manage game animations, sound effects, and user controls
  6. System Administration and Desktop Applications: System administrators use Python for scheduling tasks, background system monitoring, and creating standalone desktop applications with graphical user interfaces using toolkits like wxPython, PyQt, or Kivy.
  7. AI & Machine Learning: Python is the go-to language for AI/ML with tools such as TensorFlow, PyTorch.
  8. Desktop GUI Apps: Some of the common tools are Tkinter, PyQt.

docs.title: Related
docs.text:
Programming: It is the process of writing step-by-step instructions, known as code that tells the computer how to perform a specific task. It serves as a universal language that bridges human logic and machine operations allowing users to communicate with devices through high-level languages like Python, Java and C++.

Interpreter: It is a program that translates the high-level instructions into machine code and executes it line by line. It's a powerful tool for running Python code interactively, we can type a command and see the result immediately.

Syntax: It is a set of rules and structure that define how code must be written in a programming language so that a computer can correctly interpret and execute it. Think of it as the grammar of programming language.

Library: Is a pre-written code that can be called at any point of time.

docs.title: 1. Print function
docs.text:
print() is a function to output the text to the console. When called it evaluates any expressions supplied to it and converts values into text to be displayed.

Statement for print: print(*objects, sep=' ', end=' ')

After every print operation of each object, by default Python adds a space for separation. Similarly, after each print operation is completed, the output gets to a new line (\n).

  • objects (positional values): Accepts any number of comma separated values or expressions.
  • sep (Separator): Defines what character or string is printed between multiple arguments. Default value is space.
  • end (End-of-Line Character): Defines what character or string is printed at the very end after all values are printed. Default value is next line \n
print('cats', 'dogs', 'mice')
#Output: cats dogs mice

#Comma-Separated
print('cats', 'dogs', 'mice', sep=',')
#Output: cats,dogs,mice

#Delimit with vertical bars
print('Mozilla', 'Firefox', 'Safar', sep='|')
#Output: Mozilla|Firefox|Safari

#Tab separated alignment
print('word', 'frequency', sep='\t')
#Output: word    frequency

#Controlling line ending
print('Hello', end=' ')
print('World')
#Output: Hello World

#printing values
print(1000, 500)
#Output: 1000 500

#printing expressions
print(500 + 200)
#Output: 700

#Mixed values
print("Ramesh is", 45, "years", "old")
#Output: Ramesh is 45 years old

#String Concatenation: Joining string together using + operator
print("Hello" + "World")
#Output: HelloWorld

docs.title: 2. Data Types
docs.text:
In Python, a data type is a category for values, and every value belongs to exactly one data type. Python is object-oriented: everything is an object including numbers, strings, data structures and functions.

Variables do not explicitly require type declarations. It uses dynamic typing, where variables automatically takes on the type of the object assigned to it.

docs.title: Basic Types
docs.text:
1. Integers (int): Represents positive or negative numbers without a decimal. (-∞ to +∞)
  2. Floating-Point (float): Represents positive or negative numbers with floating point or decimal (-100.45, 567.76, 33.0).
  3. Boolean (bool): A data type strictly representing True or False.
  4. String (str): Sequence of text characters enclosed in quotes - single quote (' ') or double quotes (" ").
  5. None: A special data type denoting no value, None Type.

docs.title: Four Data Structure Types
docs.text:
1. List (list): Ordered, mutable collection (allows duplicates).
  2. Tuple (tuple): Ordered, immutable collection.
  3. Dictionary (dict): Ordered collection of key-value pairs (keys must be unique).
  4. Sets (set):Unordered collection of unique items.
Data Structure Syntax Ordered? Mutable? Duplicates? List [item1], [item2] Yes Mutable Yes Tuple (item1, item2) Yes Immutable Yes Dictionary {key:value} Unordered Mutable Keys:No, Values:Yes Set {item1}, {item2} Unordered Mutable No

Mutable: Their contents can be modified, appended, or removed. Immutable: Their contents cannot be altered once created.

docs.title: Inspecting Type with type()
docs.text:
To inspect the type of any value or variable at runtime, Python provides the built-in type() function.

x = 42
y = 55.65
z = "Hello"

print(type(x))
print(type(y))
print(type(z))

#Output: <class 'int'>
#Output: <class 'float'>
#Output: <class 'str'>

docs.title: 3. Variables
docs.text: In Python, a variable is a name that points to an object in memory — not a box that holds a value. Python is dynamically typed, so we do not need to declare the variable type - the type is inferred from the assigned value, and it can be changed later. The variable name is just a label/reference; the object carries the type.

docs.title: Naming Rules
docs.text:
1. Must start with a letter or underscore ( a-z , A-Z , _ )
  2. Cannot start with a digit
  3. Can only contain alphanumeric (letters, numbers or underscore)
  4. Names are case-sensitive
  5. Cannot be an in-built keyword

Best practice: use snake_case for multi-word names. Eg: first_name, total_price

docs.title: Assignment Patterns
docs.text:
# Multiple variables, same value
x = y = z = 0

# Multiple variables, different values
a, b, c = 1, 2, 3

docs.title: ID Function
docs.text:
The id() function returns a unique integer that identifies where the object lives in the memory for the lifetime of the object. 

a = 10
print(id(a)) #Output: Eg: 94300019145712

docs.title: 4. Python Comments
docs.text: A comment is a text in the code that Python interpreter completely ignores. It starts with # and runs to the end of the line.

docs.title: Single line comment
docs.text:
# Calculate the area of triangle
area = math.pi * radius ** 2
Comments can also be used to disable a line of code 
#print("This line is disabled")
print("This line is enabled")

docs.title: Multi-line comment
docs.text:
1. Approach 1 
    # This is a block comment
# explaining a complex algorithm.
# Each line starts with #.
  2. Approach 2 
    """
This is a multi-line block
using triple quotes.
It's ignored if not assigned to a variable.
"""

docs.title: 5. Input Function in Python
docs.text:
input() is a function to take user input. By default, the input is always stored as string. Key-point: The data entered by user (integer, float, sting) is always stored as string by default.

name = input("Enter your Name: ")
print(name)
print(type(name))
# Output:
# Enter your Name: Sam
# Sam
# <class 'str'>
when we need to accept different data type, we need to convert it using Typecasting.

docs.title: Typecasting
docs.text: Convert between data types using functions like int(), float(), str().

docs.title: Converting String
docs.text:
print(int('123'))   # string of digits parsed to integer. 
123

print(float('123')) # string parsed to float.
123.0

print(str('123'))   # str() converts anything to its text representation. Always succeeds.
123

print(bool('123'))  # only an empty string is False. Any non-empty string is True.
True                    

print(int('3.14'))  # Only works for strings that look like integers. Decimals must go through float() first.
ValueError: invalid literal for int() with base 10: '3.14'

print(float('3.14'))# string parsed to float.
3.14

print(int('Hello')) # Text like "hello" can't be cast at all.
ValueError: invalid literal for int() with base 10: 'Hello'

print(bool(""))     # only an empty string is False. Any non-empty string is True.
False

docs.title: Converting Integer
docs.text:
print(int(100))     # already an integer, no change.
100

print(float(100))   #  integer cast to float adds .0 to signal it's now a floating-point.
100.0

print(str(100))     # str() converts anything to its text representation. Always succeeds.
100

print(bool(100))    # 0 is False, every other number is True. Includes negative numbers.
True

docs.title: Converting Float
docs.text:
print(int(3.99))    # float to int truncates the decimal part (drops it, doesn't round).
3

print(float(3.99))  # already a float, no change.
3.99

print(str(3.99))    # str() converts anything to its text representation. Always succeeds.
3.99

print(bool(3.99))   # True — in Python, 0 is False, every other number is True.
True

docs.title: Converting Boolean
docs.text:
print(int(True))    # True is 1, False is 0. Reflects Python's roots in C.
1

print(float(True))  # True→1.0, False→0.0.
1.0

print(str(True))    # str() converts anything to its text representation. Always succeeds.
True

print(bool(True))   # already a boolean.
True

docs.title: Related
docs.text:
Case-sensitive: Python treats uppercase and lowercase letters as different characters. So Name, name, and NAME are three completely different identifiers.

Garbage Collector: The Garbage Collector is Python's automatic memory management system — it frees memory occupied by objects that are no longer in use, so you never have to manually delete or manage memory.

docs.title: Control Flow
docs.text: Status: In Progress

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Decision making is required when we want to execute a code only if a certain condition is satisfied.

  • In Python, the body of if statement is indicated by the indentation.
  • Body starts with an indentation and the first unindented line marks the end.

docs.title: 1. If Statement
docs.text:
Executes block if condition is True.

# Syntax
if expression:
    Body of if

# Example
number = 3
if number > 0:
    print("Its a Positive number")

print("This is always printed)

docs.title: 2. If Else Statement
docs.text:
• The if-else statement evaluates the expression and will execute the body of if only when result is True.
  • If the condition is False, body of else is executed.
  • Indentation is used to seperate the blocks.

# Syntax
if expression:
    Body of if
else:
    Body of else

# Example
number = 3
if number >= 0:
    print("Its a Positive number or Zero")
else:
    print("Its a Negative number")

docs.title: 3. If Elif & Else
docs.text:
• the elif is short for else-if. It allows us to check multiple conditions.
  • If the condition for if is False, it checks the condition of the next elif block and so on.
  • If all the condition are False, body if else is executed.
  • Only one block among all the several if..elif..else blocks is executed according to the condition.
  • The if can have only one else block. But it can have multiple elif blocks.

# Syntax
if expression:
    Body of if
elif:
    Body of elif
elif:
    Body of elif
else:
    Body of else

# Example
number = 3
if number > 0:
    print("Positive")
elif number < 0:
    print("Negative")
else:
    print("Zero")

docs.title: 4. Nested If Else
docs.text:
Conditional statements within other conditional statements.

# Syntax
if expression:
    Body of 1st if
    if expression:
        Body of 2nd if
else:
    Body of else

# Example
number = 3
if number > 0:
    print("Positive")
    if number < 0:
        print("Negative")
    else:
        print("Zero")
else:
    print("Invalid")

docs.title: Operators in Python
docs.text: Status: In Progress

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
An operator in a programming language is a symbol that performs specific mathematical, relational or logical operation and produces a final result.

An expression consists of operators and operands operators + operands = expression

Example: 5 + 3 = 8 Here 5 & 3 are Operands, '+' is the Operator

docs.title: 1. Arithmetic Operators
docs.text:
Arithmetic operators are used to perform mathematical operations like

  1. Addition (+) : Performs addition
  2. Subtraction (-) : Performs subtraction
  3. Multiplication (*) : Performs multiplication
  4. Division (/) : Performs division and the result is always retured as decimal number.
  5. Modulus (%) : Performs the division and returns the reminder.
  6. Floor Division (//) : Performs division and the result is floored to nearest smaller integer.
  7. Power (**) : Performs power of function
print(10 + 3)       # both operands int, result stays int.
13

print(10 / 3)       # both operands int, result stays float. 
3.333333333

print(10 // 3)      # both operands int, result stays int.
3

print(-8 // 3)      # both operands int, result stays int.
-3

print(10 % 3)       # both operands int, result stays int.
1

print(2 ** 0.5)     # mixed int/float ⇒ result is float. 
1.414213

print("Hi "*3)      # Python's neat trick. Multiplies the string n times.
Hi Hi Hi 

print("abc"+"def")  # Python concatenates the strings. Result type stays string.
abcdef

print(2.5 + True)   # booleans are treated as integers in arithmetic.
3.5

print("1" + 1)      # Python does NOT auto-convert. You must explicitly cast
TypeError: can only concatenate str (not "int") to str

print(5 + None)     # None has no arithmetic operations defined.
TypeError: unsupported operand type(s) for +: 'int' and 'NoneType'

print("Hi " * 2.5)  # string multiplication only works with INTEGER counts.
TypeError: cant multiply sequence by non-int

print(int(3.25 // 1))   # floors to 3
3

print(-4.25 // 1)   # floors to -5.0
-5.0

print(5 // 1)       # floors to same number 5
5

docs.title: BODMAS Rule
docs.text:
In Python, BODMAS rule is used to determine the order of operations for mathematical expressions.

  • Brackets (): Have the highest precedence and are evaluated first.
  • Division (/) and Multiplication (*): Have equal precedence and are evaluated from left to right.
  • Addition (+) and Subtraction (-): Have equal precedence and are evaluated from left to right.

docs.title: 2. Comparison Operators
docs.text:
These operators are used to perform comparison and the result is always a boolean: True or False

Operator Name Example == Is Equal To 3 == 5 gives us False != Not Equal To 3 != 5 gives us True > Greater Than 3 > 5 gives us False < Less Than 3 < 5 gives us True >= Greater Than or Equal To 3 >= 5 gives us False <= Lesser Than or Equal To 3 <= 5 gives us True 
2 == 2.0        # int and float ARE compatible. Python auto-converts the int to float, then compares the values numerically.
True

2 == "2"        # Python does NOT auto-convert between numbers and strings.
False

2 == None       # None is equal only to itself. Any other comparison with None for equality is False.
False

False == 0      # booleans are treated as integers:True = 1, False = 0
True

True == 1       # booleans are treated as integers:True = 1, False = 0
True

"ABC" == "abc"  # straightforward same-type comparison.
False

"abc" != "abd"  # straightforward same-type comparison.
True

2 < "2"         # int and str cannot be ordered. Python won't auto-convert. 
TypeError: '<' not supported between instances of 'int' and 'str'

2 < 2.0001      # int and float ARE compatible.
True

100 >= 32       # straightforward same-type comparison.
True

2 == 2.00001    # int and float ARE compatible.
False

docs.title: 3. Assignment Operators
docs.text:
These operators are used to assign value to the variables.

Operator Name Example = Assignment Operator a = 7 += Addition Assignment a += 1 #a = a + 1 -= Subtraction Assignment a -= 2 #a = a - 2 *= Multiplication Assignment a *= 4 #a = a * 4 /= Division Assignment a /= 5 #a = a / 5 %= Reminder Assignment a %= 6 #a = a % 6 **= Exponent Assignment a **= 7 #a = a ** 7

docs.title: 4. Logical Operators
docs.text:
These operations are used to check whether the expression is True or False. They are used to evaluate conditions in decision-making.

Operator Name Example and a and b True only of both the operands are True or a or b True if atleast one of operands is True not not a True if the operant is False and vice-versa A B A and B True True True True False False False True False False False False A B A or B True True True True False True False True True False False False

Usecase 1: if user is not None and user.is_admin - never errors even when user is None. Usecase 2: if file_exists(path) and read(path) - only reads if the file exists.

docs.title: 5. Special Operators
docs.text:
There are two special operators "is" and "in"

  1. Identity Operator (is) It tells you if both the objects are at the same memory location.

  2. Membership Operator (in) It tells you if an object is part of another object or not.
